clinicalPearls: Presents as tender, red, indurated nodules or plaques, often on the trunk and proximal limbs, that may ulcerate and discharge oily fluid
Lesions are frequently provoked by trauma at the affected site
It is a rare cutaneous manifestation of alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, most strongly linked to the severe PiZZ phenotype
Look for associated features of the deficiency such as early-onset emphysema and liver disease
Biopsy shows a neutrophilic lobular (and often septal) panniculitis with splaying of neutrophils between dermal collagen bundles and liquefactive fat necrosis
Serum alpha-1-antitrypsin level and phenotype/genotype confirm the diagnosis
Treatment centres on alpha-1-antitrypsin replacement/augmentation therapy in severe disease, with dapsone often used for milder cases
reference.pathophysiology: Alpha-1-antitrypsin is the principal circulating inhibitor of neutrophil-derived proteases such as elastase. In deficiency states, particularly the PiZZ phenotype, unopposed protease activity in the subcutaneous fat leads to uncontrolled tissue and connective-tissue breakdown when neutrophils are recruited, often after minor trauma. The resulting neutrophilic panniculitis features destruction of collagen and adipose tissue with liquefactive necrosis, and the loss of protease inhibition allows the inflammatory process to become self-perpetuating and destructive.
additionalInvestigations: Deep incisional biopsy including subcutaneous fat with tissue culture to exclude infection
Liver function tests and assessment for hepatic involvement
Pulmonary function tests for associated emphysema
Full blood count and inflammatory markers
redFlags: Extensive ulceration with rapid tissue destruction and secondary sepsis
Evidence of associated severe emphysema or progressive liver disease
Failure to respond to standard treatment, warranting augmentation therapy
Recurrent lesions at sites of minor trauma indicating ongoing uncontrolled protease activity
reference.prognosis: The panniculitis often follows a chronic relapsing course and can be difficult to control, but replacement of alpha-1-antitrypsin can produce marked improvement in severe cases. Overall outlook is also shaped by the associated pulmonary and hepatic manifestations of the deficiency.
pitfalls: Not measuring alpha-1-antitrypsin levels and phenotype in a neutrophilic panniculitis
Interpreting a normal level during acute inflammation without recognising it is an acute-phase reactant that can be falsely raised
Mistaking the neutrophilic infiltrate for infection and withholding appropriate therapy
Overlooking associated pulmonary and hepatic disease
management: Intravenous augmentation therapy with pooled human alpha-1-antitrypsin can produce marked improvement in severe or refractory panniculitis
Dapsone is commonly used first-line for its anti-neutrophil action, after screening for G6PD deficiency
Avoid trauma to susceptible skin, which can provoke new lesions
Provide wound care for ulcerating, oily-discharging nodules and treat any secondary infection
Assess and manage the associated pulmonary emphysema and hepatic manifestations of the deficiency
Coordinate care across dermatology, respiratory and metabolic teams, and consider liver transplantation in appropriate cases, which can also resolve the panniculitis
Offer genetic counselling and family screening
